## The 3x Problem

<p class="big-idea">The coding got faster<br><span class="accent-orange">The rest of it didn't (mostly...)</span></p>

## The 3x Developer

- Most corporate devs are here right now (?)
- Planning with AI help
- Coding with Cursor, Codex, or Claude
    - From the most to least expensive task
- An `AGENTS.md`
- Tried a skill or two: `/superpowers`, `/grill-me`, etc.
- Used `/review` or CodeRabbit, GitHub, Copilot

## `AGENTS.md` : "Agentic Employee 101"

- Explains where everything is and what it does
- Build, test, review commands
- Every agent the same starting point
- Subdirectories too
- "Prefer integration tests, vertical-slice tests, and smoke tests that exercise
  real feature boundaries over narrow unit tests with little incremental value."
- `/init`
- Delete it?  Update it?

<p class="big-idea">Don't prompt the rules, record them</p>

## Skills: The Basic Structure

```text
my-skill/
├── SKILL.md
├── scripts/
│   └── do_the_work.py
├── references/
└── assets/
```

<p class="plain-note"><code>SKILL.md</code> explains when to use the skill. The supporting files make the work repeatable.</p>

## Skills save Tokens

![](screenshots/token-cost.png){.slide-image fig-alt="Token usage and cost showing approximately 286 million tokens and 191 dollars"}

## Skills: Keep Them Thin

- Small Python scripts do the actual work
- Each thin skill is easy to run, test, and repair
- Repeatable behavior
- Python doesn't burn tokens...
- Explicit triggers: "Use $slack-skill to send `hi folks`"
- Implicit triggers: "Send this message `hi folks`"

## Preflight Skill

- Setup and Auth the MCPs and local services the workflow needs
- Run at startup, and when something fails
- Report status

## Orchestration: It's just a skill

- Delegates to thin skills to do the work
- A recipe book of behaviors/autonomous
- I made: Developer, Reviewer and Submitter

## Skill Hierarchy

```text
project/
└── .agents/
    └── skills/
        └── orchestrator.md
            ├── jira/
            ├── coding/
            ├── slack/
            ├── perforce/       # source control
            ├── swarm/          # reviews
            └── preflight/
```

<p class="plain-note"><code>orchestrator.md</code> chooses the workflow and delegates each step to a child skill.</p>

## Orchestration: Autonomous Developer

- 10: Find a case to work on (auto or directed)
- Take ownership in Jira, In Progress
- Implement it
- Run tests/checks
- Send to Swarm for review
- Open a slack thread with details
- Goto 10

<svg class="reviewer-loop" viewBox="0 0 1000 430" role="img" aria-label="Autonomous reviewer loop. Read Review branches to Fix Obvious Problems or Human Help. Both paths continue to Post Slack and Swarm Update, then Queue Tests, which loops back to Read Review.">

<p class="big-idea"><span class="accent">Huge Time Saver</span></p>

## Orchestration: Autonomous Reviewer

- 10: Read Swarm (review comments)
- Make a judgement call
- Auto fix, or defer to human
- Fix bug / feature
- Update the review
- Update automated tests
- Post to Swarm and the Slack thread
- Goto 10

## Orchestration: Submitter

- Check the CL tests
- Wait for test validation
- Submit
- Post to Slack thread
- Mark bug complete

## The 10x Developer Target

- Automation is spread throughout
- You still read code
- Your day job is planning, reviewing and testing
- The agent is your intern, doing all the boring bits

## The 100x Developer

- Most code is no longer read by a human
- Agents work on the whole problem (autonomously?)
- Parallel workflows, multiple agents
- The code is a black box (agents can test)
- The inputs and outputs are checked by humans and agents
- You are an Architect, an Orchestrator, a Detective

## Small Slices, Frequent Checks

<div class="checkpoint-strip">
  <div class="checkpoint"><strong>Plan</strong>One visible outcome<span class="check">✓ Check intent</span></div>
  <div class="checkpoint"><strong>Build</strong>One small diff<span class="check">✓ Read the code</span></div>
  <div class="checkpoint"><strong>Prove</strong>Tests and evidence<span class="check">✓ Check behavior</span></div>
  <div class="checkpoint"><strong>Ship</strong>A safe deployment<span class="check">✓ Check reality</span></div>
</div>

<p class="plain-note">Small enough to understand. Complete enough to matter.</p>

## The Agent Needs Eyes

<div class="card-grid four">
  <div class="idea-card green"><strong>Logs</strong>What happened?</div>
  <div class="idea-card green"><strong>Screenshots</strong>What changed?</div>
  <div class="idea-card green"><strong>Tests</strong>Does it still work?</div>
  <div class="idea-card green"><strong>Preview</strong>Does it work for real?</div>
</div>

<p class="big-idea">If the agent cannot see the result,<br><span class="accent-orange">you have to check it manually.</span></p>

## Prompts Don't Compound

- A prompt buys one answer
- A test prevents the same failure forever
- A script makes the result repeatable
- A skill makes the workflow reusable

<p class="big-idea"><span class="accent-orange">Chat history is not infrastructure.</span></p>

## Debug Dumps

- One command captures errors, logs, settings, and state
- The agent reads the dump instead of asking you twenty questions
- Fix, rerun, compare

<p class="big-idea">Ask the program.<br><span class="accent">Not the tired human.</span></p>

## Image Grabs

- Capture the screen at known points
- Attach the image to the task automatically
- Let the agent inspect the real result

<p class="plain-note">“It looks wrong” becomes evidence instead of a conversation.</p>

## Image Diffs

- Keep a trusted “before”
- Render the new version
- Highlight only the changed pixels
- Stop if something unexpected moved

<p class="big-idea"><span class="accent">Show the difference.</span> Skip the guessing.</p>

## Audio Comparisons

- Render the reference and the new output
- Compare volume, timing, silence, and shape
- Make failures visible as a waveform

<p class="big-idea">Some bugs have to be <span class="accent-orange">heard.</span></p>

## Client/Server Round Trip

- Start the real client and server
- Send a real request
- Capture both sides of the conversation
- Fail if either side disagrees

<p class="plain-note">A unit test can pass while the product is still broken.</p>

## Lean Correctness Specs

- Use Lean to specify the correctness of the result.

## Iterative Goals

- Give the agent one clear finish line
- Let it work, test, and correct itself
- Keep the goal alive across many steps
- Stop only on evidence—or a real blocker

## Vertical Slices

- One small behavior, end to end
- UI, logic, test, and deployment together
- Useful enough to try
- Small enough to understand and revert

<p class="big-idea">Do not build three layers.<br><span class="accent">Build one working thing.</span></p>

## Incremental Steps for the Human

- Each step leaves a readable diff
- Each step leaves test evidence
- Each step leaves a short summary
- You can interrupt without losing the plot

## Quick Prototypes

- Ugly but runnable beats perfect but imaginary
- Test the risky idea first
- Throw it away without regret

<p class="plain-note">The prototype answers a question. It is not a promise.</p>

## Small attack surfaces

- Give the agent the smallest useful task
- Limit files, tools, permissions, and scope
- Prefer reversible changes
- Fewer ways to be wrong means faster trust

## Insane build speeds

- Slow feedback creates large, risky guesses
- Fast feedback lets the agent correct itself
- Seconds invite experiments
- Minutes invite waiting

<p class="big-idea">Build speed is not comfort.<br><span class="accent">It is control.</span></p>

## Presentation Fun

## Code Inspection

- Ask for a map, not a guided tour
- Find entry points, data flow, rules, and sharp edges
- Write the map down
- Review the map before changing the code

## 75/25 Rule

- 25%: solve today's problem
- 75%: remove the friction that made it hard
- Add the missing test
- Improve the tool
- Capture the instruction

<p class="big-idea">Ship the fix.<br><span class="accent">Then improve the factory.</span></p>

## Dog Food

- Use the workflow on real work
- Notice every manual rescue
- Put that friction into the backlog
- Run it again until the rescue disappears

## Scriptify

- If you explain it twice, make it a command
- Clear inputs
- Clear output
- Useful exit codes
- Safe to rerun

<p class="big-idea">A script is a tiny tool<br>that never forgets the steps.</p>
